claims.text: In four cities over eight summers, heat-related emergency department visits were lower on heat alert days (rate ratio 0.83, 95 percent CI 0.74 to 0.93).
claims.passage: Heat-related emergency department visits were lower on alert days (rate ratio 0.83, 95 percent CI 0.74 to 0.93).
claims.interpretation: Activation is associated with fewer heat-related visits; confounding by temperature remains possible.

claims.text: In one region, the mean cost of a heat-health activation day was 42,000, and no cost per emergency visit avoided could be calculated because health effects were not estimated.
claims.passage: The mean cost per activation day was 42,000, of which cooling centres accounted for more than half.
claims.interpretation: Costs are known locally; value for money is not.

claims.text: Lowering the activation threshold by 2 degrees raised activation days from 6 to 14 per summer, and heat-related emergency visits on the newly covered days were 9 percent below expected with an interval from -3 to 20 percent.
claims.passage: On the newly covered days, heat-related emergency department visits were 9 percent below the number expected from the previous threshold's pattern (95 percent CI -3 to 20 percent).
claims.interpretation: The benefit of a lower threshold is uncertain and includes no effect.

claims.text: On alert days, heat-related visit rates were 2.4 times higher in the lowest income fifth, where the reduction associated with alerts was smaller.
claims.passage: On alert days, visit rates were 2.4 times higher in the lowest income fifth than in the highest.
claims.interpretation: Public alerts alone reach low-income neighbourhoods least; targeting matters.

claims.text: Of 22 studies of heat-health warning systems, none was randomised and only 5 examined emergency department visits or ambulance calls.
claims.passage: Only 5 studies examined emergency department visits or ambulance calls, with mixed results.
claims.interpretation: The evidence base is observational and thin for emergency care.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Time-series evidence associates heat alerts with fewer heat-related emergency visits, but a review of 22 non-randomised studies found only 5 on emergency care, with mixed results. Lowering the threshold more than doubled activation days in one unit, with an uncertain effect on visits whose interval includes none. A regional costing gives the cost of an activation day but no health effect, so value for money cannot be computed. Older people living alone and low-income neighbourhoods benefit least from public alerts; outreach calls and transport to cooling centres help.
gradeRationale: Observational time-series and before-after evidence with possible confounding by temperature; the threshold evidence is imprecise; costs are known but not linked to effects.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five claims, one of high uncertainty; certainty low.
